INTERPRETATIONMake your own read first, then show the stepwise interpretation

    Course teaching rules: normal is 80–120% of predicted; TLC below 80% is small lungs and above 120% big lungs; FEV1/FVC below 70% is obstruction; DLCO below 80% is low; a bronchodilator response is a rise in FEV1 or FVC of more than 10% of predicted (the ERS/ATS 2022 criterion). Clinical labs compare each value with a lower limit of normal from reference equations instead of fixed percentages.

    HOW THE TESTS WORK

    Spirometry

    The patient breathes through a flow sensor; volume is flow added up over time. Spirometry measures what moves in and out (tidal volume, IRV, ERV, vital capacity) but never the air that stays in the lungs, so RV, FRC, and TLC need another test.

    After the first quarter of the vital capacity is out, pushing harder no longer raises flow. Why? As the patient pushes, pleural pressure squeezes the airways. Where the pressure inside an airway falls below the pleural pressure outside it, the airway is compressed: that is the flow-limiting segment. Pushing harder compresses it more, so flow stops rising. As the lung empties, the flow-limiting segment moves into smaller airways, and what is left to drive flow is the lung's own elastic recoil. That is why maximal flow falls as the lung empties (less recoil), why emphysema scoops the curve (less recoil and floppy airways), and why fibrosis can keep flows high for its volume (more recoil).

    Model detail, beyond the course: the simulator computes that limit as the lung's recoil pressure divided by the resistance of the small airways upstream of the flow-limiting segment, V̇max = Pel(V) / Rus.

    Body box plethysmography

    Diffusing capacity (DLCO)

    The patient inhales a small amount of carbon monoxide with an inert tracer gas, holds for 10 seconds, and exhales. The analyzer measures how much CO disappeared; dilution of the tracer gives the alveolar volume it was spread through. CO has to cross the alveolar membrane and then bind hemoglobin, two steps in series, so their resistances add:

    1 / DLCO = 1 / DM + 1 / (θ · Vc)

    Emphysema destroys membrane and capillaries; fibrosis thickens the membrane; anemia lowers θ (less hemoglobin to bind CO), which is why the report also gives a hemoglobin-corrected value. Asthma and obesity spare the alveoli, so DLCO stays normal or high.

    Model details.

    • Lung volumes come from the Statics page (lung, chest wall, and muscle curves).
    • Forced expiratory flow is the smallest of three limits: Pel/Rus, expiratory effort, and a central-airway maximum. Rus rises when the small airways are narrowed and when lung recoil falls (the airways lose their tethering).
    • Beyond the course: the airways count as closed where Rus reaches ten times its normal open value. That volume sets RV when it is above the chest wall limit (closure begins a little higher, at the closing capacity), which is how air trapping raises RV in emphysema and in an asthma attack. In a forced expiration the airways are also squeezed, so they close earlier (at seven times the open value); that is why SVC exceeds FVC in obstruction.
    • Beyond the course: when the small airways cannot carry a quiet expiration (about 0.5 L/s) at the relaxed FRC, the patient breathes at a higher volume, so the measured FRC rises (dynamic hyperinflation).
    • Raw is the body box airway resistance at FRC, mostly from the central airways.
    • DLCO assumes membrane and blood conductances in the ratio the ERS/ATS hemoglobin correction is built on, with a reference hemoglobin of 14.6 g/dL. θ is the rate at which hemoglobin takes up CO.
    • The test ends when flow stays below 25 mL/s for 1 s (ERS/ATS 2019) or at 15 s.
    • The obesity patient’s stiff chest wall stands in for the effects of mass loading; measured chest wall compliance is close to normal in obesity (Behazin 2010).
    • The weakness patient’s muscles are at 30% of normal strength, and the lung and chest wall are also stiffer (0.8 and 0.85 of normal), as measured in chronic weakness (Gibson 1977; Estenne 1983). Beyond the course: weak muscles alone cost less volume than you might expect, because TLC sits where the lung’s curve is nearly flat; in patients, stiffer tissues add to the loss (De Troyer 1980).
    • Not modeled: effort variability, the chest wall changes of aging, gas dilution lung volumes, and the effect of alveolar volume on DLCO (KCO).
